title: Πείσανδρος καὶ Ἁρπαλίων
about: Antilochus, taking aim in the throng, is stabbed at by Adamas, but Poseidon blunts the spear on his shield; Adamas draws back, and Meriones follows and wounds him in the lower belly, and he dies. Helenus strikes the helmet from Deipyrus, and Menelaus, grieved, goes for him; they cast together, Helenus’ arrow bounces off Menelaus’ breastplate, and Menelaus’ spear pins Helenus’ bow-hand to the bow, so that Agenor draws it out and binds the hand with a sling. Peisander then charges Menelaus, his spear fails against the shield, and Menelaus kills him with a sword-blow to the forehead and, standing over him, tells the Trojans that they cannot have enough of war and reproaches Zeus for favouring them. Harpalion, a son of the Paphlagonian king Pylaemenes, thrusts at Menelaus’ shield and fails, and Meriones kills him with an arrow as he retreats; the Paphlagonians carry him to Ilium, his father weeping beside the chariot.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ λῆθ’ Ἀδάμαντα τιτυσκόμενος καθ’ ὅμιλον
Ἀσιάδην, ὅ οἱ οὖτα μέσον σάκος ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ
ἐγγύθεν ὁρμηθείς·
sentences.i: But as he took aim through the throng, he did not escape Adamas, the son of Asius, who rushed upon him and stabbed the middle of his shield with sharp bronze from close by;
sentences.n: The man taking aim is Antilochus, the last figure of the previous part; the Greek does not name him until 565, and the man who stabs his shield is Adamas. λῆθ’ is ἔληθε, the unaugmented aorist of λανθάνω, which takes the person who fails to notice as its object: τιτυσκόμενος ‘aiming’ (nominative, Antilochus) did not escape the notice of Ἀδάμαντα (accusative). Ἀσιάδην ‘son of Asius’ is a patronymic in apposition to it. ὅ is the relative ‘who’, οἱ ‘his’, and οὖτα is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘stab, wound’. καθ’ ὅμιλον ‘through the throng’. ὁρμηθείς is the aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω, active in sense: ‘having rushed’ (compare the infinitive ὁρμηθῆναι at 559). The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀμενήνωσεν δέ οἱ αἰχμὴν
κυανοχαῖτα Ποσειδάων βιότοιο μεγήρας.
sentences.l:
and made powerless for him the point,
dark-haired Poseidon, begrudging life.
sentences.i: but dark-haired Poseidon, begrudging Antilochus his life, made the point of Adamas’ spear powerless.
sentences.n: Poseidon is protecting Antilochus. ἀμενήνωσεν is the aorist of ἀμενηνόω ‘make ἀμενηνός, powerless’ (the adjective looks built on ἀ- ‘not’ and μένος ‘might’), οἱ ‘for him’ is Adamas, and αἰχμήν is the ‘point’ of his spear. μεγήρας is the aorist participle of μεγαίρω ‘begrudge’, which takes the thing grudged in the genitive: βιότοιο, epic genitive of βίοτος ‘life’. Whose life is grudged the Greek does not say; it can only be Antilochus’, so `i` names him. κυανοχαῖτα is the nominative of κυανοχαίτης ‘dark-haired’ in its epic form with -α, the god’s stock epithet. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸ μὲν αὐτοῦ μεῖν’ ὥς τε σκῶλος πυρίκαυστος
ἐν σάκει Ἀντιλόχοιο, τὸ δ’ ἥμισυ κεῖτ’ ἐπὶ γαίης·
sentences.l:
And one part of it stayed, like a fire-burnt stake,
in the shield of Antilochus, and the half lay on the earth;
sentences.i: One part of it stayed in Antilochus’ shield like a stake burnt in the fire, and the other half lay on the ground;
sentences.n: The spear has broken: one part, with the point, sticks in the shield, and the other half falls. The Greek does not say which part is which; τὸ μὲν αὐτοῦ is ‘that part of it’, and τὸ δ’ ἥμισυ ‘the half’. μεῖν’ is μεῖνε, unaugmented aorist of μένω ‘stay’, elided; κεῖτ’ is κεῖτο ‘lay’. σκῶλος is a rare word, usually taken to mean a pointed stake, and πυρίκαυστος is ‘burnt in fire’ (the usual explanation is a stake hardened in the fire); the exact meaning of σκῶλος is not certain. ὥς τε ‘like’.

sentences.t: ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων·
sentences.l: and back to the company of his companions he drew away, death-fate avoiding;
sentences.i: and he drew back into the company of his companions, shunning death.
sentences.n: Adamas, his spear blunted, retreats; the line is a formula that recurs at 596 (Helenus) and 648 (Harpalion) and stands also at 3.32, and it is translated the same each time. ἂψ ‘back’; ἑτάρων is ἑταίρων ‘companions’ (epic spelling) and ἔθνος ‘company, body of people’; ἐχάζετο is the imperfect middle of χάζομαι ‘draw back, give ground’. κῆρ’ is κῆρα, elided, the accusative of κήρ ‘death-fate’, which is a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’; ἀλεείνων ‘avoiding, shunning’, from ἀλεείνω.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δ’ ἀπιόντα μετασπόμενος βάλε δουρὶ
αἰδοίων τε μεσηγὺ καὶ ὀμφαλοῦ, ἔνθα μάλιστα
γίγνετ’ Ἄρης ἀλεγεινὸς ὀϊζυροῖσι βροτοῖσιν.
sentences.l:
And Meriones, following after him as he went away, hit him with a spear
between the genitals and the navel, where most
becomes Ares grievous for sorrowful mortals.
sentences.i: And Meriones, following after him as he went away, struck him with his spear between the genitals and the navel, where war is most grievous to sorrowful mortals.
sentences.n: Meriones wounds Adamas in the lower belly as he retreats. ἀπιόντα ‘him going away’, accusative participle of ἄπειμι, is Adamas; μετασπόμενος ‘following after’ is the aorist middle participle of the verb ἕπομαι ‘follow’ with μετα- ‘after’ (the simple form ἑσπόμενος comes at 570). δουρί is the dative of δόρυ ‘spear’, ‘with a spear’. αἰδοίων is the genitive of αἰδοῖα, ‘the parts of shame’, the genitals; μεσηγύ ‘between’ takes it and ὀμφαλοῦ ‘navel’. The last line is a general remark: at this spot, Ἄρης (the god, standing for war and its work) ‘becomes’ ἀλεγεινός ‘grievous’ most of all for ὀϊζυροῖσι βροτοῖσιν ‘sorrowful mortals’, i.e. a wound there is the worst to bear.

sentences.t: ἔνθά οἱ ἔγχος ἔπηξεν·
sentences.l: There in him the spear he fixed;
sentences.i: There he fixed his spear in him.
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ is the spot just named, and οἱ ‘in him’ is Adamas, in the dative; ἔπηξεν is the aorist of πήγνυμι ‘fix, plant’. ἔγχος is a spear, as δόρυ is in the line before: the two words are translated alike. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἑσπόμενος περὶ δουρὶ
ἤσπαιρ’ ὡς ὅτε βοῦς τόν τ’ οὔρεσι βουκόλοι ἄνδρες
ἰλλάσιν οὐκ ἐθέλοντα βίῃ δήσαντες ἄγουσιν·
sentences.i: and he, following the spear, writhed about it, as when cowherds in the mountains bind an unwilling ox by force with ropes and lead it away;
sentences.n: A simile for a dying man struggling on a spear: he is like an ox that does not want to go and is bound and dragged. ἑσπόμενος ‘following’ is the aorist middle participle of ἕπομαι ‘follow’; the Greek does not say how he follows the spear, only that he is pulled along with it and writhes περὶ δουρί ‘about the spear’. ἤσπαιρ’ is ἤσπαιρε, imperfect of ἀσπαίρω ‘gasp, struggle convulsively’, said of the dying; ‘writhed’ fits a body twisting against a spear and an animal against ropes. The simile is built with ὡς ὅτε ‘as when’; τόν τ’ is the relative ‘which’ with epic τε; οὔρεσι is ὄρεσι ‘in the mountains’; βουκόλοι ἄνδρες ‘cowherd men’. ἰλλάσιν is the dative plural of ἰλλάς, a rare word for a rope, probably related to εἰλέω ‘twist’. δήσαντες is the aorist participle of δέω ‘bind’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ τυπεὶς ἤσπαιρε μίνυνθά περ, οὔ τι μάλα δήν,
ὄφρά οἱ ἐκ χροὸς ἔγχος ἀνεσπάσατ’ ἐγγύθεν ἐλθὼν
ἥρως Μηριόνης·
sentences.i: So he writhed when struck, only a little while, not long at all, until the hero Meriones came up close and pulled the spear out of his flesh;
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ answers the ὡς ὅτε of the simile. μίνυνθά περ, οὔ τι μάλα δήν is a formula for a short time (‘for a little while, not very long at all’), the same words as in the Odyssey. τυπείς is the aorist passive participle of τύπτω ‘strike’. ὄφρα with the aorist ἀνεσπάσατ’ (= ἀνεσπάσατο, middle of ἀνασπάω ‘pull up, pull out’) means ‘until’; χροός is the genitive of χρώς ‘flesh, skin’; ἐγγύθεν ἐλθών ‘having come from close by’. ἥρως ‘hero’ is Meriones’ title, in apposition to the name. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε.
sentences.l: and darkness covered his two eyes.
sentences.i: and darkness covered his eyes.
sentences.n: This is the stock line for the moment of death, as at 4.461, 4.503 and 4.526: Adamas is dead. τόν ‘him’ is the whole man and ὄσσε the part, his ‘two eyes’ (ὄσσε is a dual), both in the accusative after κάλυψε, the aorist of καλύπτω ‘cover’. σκότος is ‘darkness’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
Δηΐπυρον δ’ Ἕλενος ξίφεϊ σχεδὸν ἤλασε κόρσην
Θρηϊκίῳ μεγάλῳ, ἀπὸ δὲ τρυφάλειαν ἄραξεν.
sentences.l:
And Deipyrus Helenus with his sword struck at close quarters on the temple,
a great Thracian one, and knocked the helm off.
sentences.i: And Helenus struck Deipyrus on the temple at close quarters with a great Thracian sword, and knocked off his helmet.
sentences.n: Helenus (a son of Priam, as 586 shows) strikes down Deipyrus, a man the poem does not describe; that he is an Achaean follows from the next lines, where an Achaean picks up his helmet and Menelaus grieves. Δηΐπυρον is the accusative object of ἤλασε, the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, here ‘strike’; κόρσην ‘on the temple’ is the part struck, in the accusative. ξίφεϊ is the dative of ξίφος ‘sword’, with Θρηϊκίῳ μεγάλῳ ‘Thracian, great’; σχεδόν ‘at close quarters’. ἀπὸ … ἄραξεν is split in two (a tmesis): ἀράσσω ‘strike hard’ with ἀπό ‘off’, ‘knocked off’. τρυφάλεια is a word for a helmet whose origin is not known.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἀποπλαγχθεῖσα χαμαὶ πέσε, καί τις Ἀχαιῶν
μαρναμένων μετὰ ποσσὶ κυλινδομένην ἐκόμισσε·
sentences.l:
That one, driven off, fell to the ground, and some one of the Achaeans
who were fighting picked it up as it rolled among their feet;
sentences.i: The helmet, driven off, fell to the ground, and one of the fighting Achaeans picked it up as it rolled among their feet;
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν ‘that one’ is the helmet, set against the man in the next line (τὸν δέ). ἀποπλαγχθεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of ἀποπλάζω ‘drive off’. καί τις Ἀχαιῶν ‘and some one of the Achaeans’ takes μαρναμένων ‘who were fighting’ (genitive plural) with it. μετὰ ποσσί ‘among the feet’ goes with κυλινδομένην ‘as it rolled’ (accusative, agreeing with the helmet). ἐκόμισσε is the aorist of κομίζω ‘take charge of, carry’, here ‘took up’. ποσσί is the epic dative plural of πούς.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ἐρεβεννὴ νὺξ ἐκάλυψεν.
sentences.l: and over his eyes the murky night covered him.
sentences.i: and murky night covered him over his eyes.
sentences.n: τόν is Deipyrus, whom Helenus has struck on the temple; the line is the same as 5.659 (with a movable ν on ἐκάλυψεν) and says that night closes over a man’s eyes. Unlike τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε at 575, it does not say that he dies, and the poem does not say what happens to Deipyrus. ἐρεβεννή ‘murky’ is built on Ἔρεβος ‘darkness’; κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν is ‘down over his eyes’, with the genitive.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδην δ’ ἄχος εἷλε βοὴν ἀγαθὸν Μενέλαον·
sentences.l: And Atreus’-son grief seized, Menelaus good at the war-cry;
sentences.i: Grief seized the son of Atreus, Menelaus, good at the war-cry.
sentences.n: Menelaus is the one meant: Ἀτρεΐδην ‘son of Atreus’ is the patronymic and Μενέλαον the name, both in the accusative, since ἄχος εἷλε ‘grief seized’ takes its object so. The grief is for Deipyrus, just struck down. ἄχος is ‘grief’ and εἷλε the aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize’. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἐπαπειλήσας Ἑλένῳ ἥρωϊ ἄνακτι
ὀξὺ δόρυ κραδάων·
sentences.l:
and he went, threatening Helenus, the hero lord,
swinging a sharp spear;
sentences.i: and he went against the hero lord Helenus, with threats, swinging a sharp spear;
sentences.n: Menelaus goes for Helenus, the man who struck Deipyrus. ἐπαπειλήσας is the aorist participle of ἐπαπειλέω ‘threaten’, with the dative Ἑλένῳ for the man threatened; βῆ ‘went’ is the aorist of βαίνω. ἥρωϊ ἄνακτι ‘the hero lord’ gives Helenus’ rank: ἄναξ ‘lord’ is the title of a prince. ὀξὺ δόρυ is ‘a sharp spear’ and κραδάων the participle of κραδάω ‘swing, brandish’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ τόξου πῆχυν ἄνελκε.
sentences.l: and the other the arm of the bow drew back.
sentences.i: while the other drew back the bow.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’, the other, is Helenus, who is drawing his bow. πῆχυς is the word for the forearm; what part of the bow it names is not agreed, and the English leaves it at ‘bow’. ἄνελκε is the imperfect of ἀνέλκω ‘draw back’, without augment; it shows the drawing is going on while Menelaus approaches. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἄρ’ ὁμαρτήδην ὃ μὲν ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι
ἵετ’ ἀκοντίσσαι, ὃ δ’ ἀπὸ νευρῆφιν ὀϊστῷ.
sentences.l:
And those two together, the one with a sharp spear
was eager to cast, the other from the string with an arrow.
sentences.i: And the two, together, were both eager to cast, the one with a sharp spear, the other with an arrow from the bowstring.
sentences.n: Menelaus (spear) and Helenus (bow) let go at the same instant. τώ is the dual ‘the two’; ὁμαρτήδην ‘together, at the same moment’; ὃ μὲν … ὃ δέ ‘the one … the other’. ἵετ’ is ἵετο, imperfect middle of ἵημι ‘be eager’, with the infinitive ἀκοντίσσαι (ἀκοντίσαι with the double σ for the metre), ‘to cast’. The second half has no verb of its own and takes the same one: ‘the other (was eager to cast) with an arrow’. ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι ‘with a sharp spear’; ἀπὸ νευρῆφιν ‘from the string’ (-φιν is an old ending; νευρή is the bowstring); ὀϊστῷ ‘with an arrow’.

sentences.t:
Πριαμίδης μὲν ἔπειτα κατὰ στῆθος βάλεν ἰῷ
θώρηκος γύαλον, ἀπὸ δ’ ἔπτατο πικρὸς ὀϊστός.
sentences.l:
Priam’s-son then on the chest hit with the arrow,
the hollow of the breastplate, and off flew the bitter arrow.
sentences.i: The son of Priam hit him then on the chest with the arrow, on the hollow of the breastplate, and the bitter arrow flew off.
sentences.n: Helenus’ arrow strikes Menelaus’ breastplate and glances away, which the simile that follows pictures. Πριαμίδης ‘son of Priam’ is Helenus; the Greek does not name the man hit, but it can only be Menelaus. κατὰ στῆθος is ‘on the chest’, and ἰῷ the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’ (the word also means poison, but here it is the arrow named again in the next line). θώρηκος γύαλον ‘the hollow of the breastplate’ is the curved plate over the chest. ἀπὸ … ἔπτατο is a tmesis, ‘flew off’, the aorist of πέτομαι; πικρός ‘bitter’ is the stock word for an arrow.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀπὸ πλατέος πτυόφιν μεγάλην κατ’ ἀλωὴν
θρῴσκωσιν κύαμοι μελανόχροες ἢ ἐρέβινθοι
πνοιῇ ὕπο λιγυρῇ καὶ λικμητῆρος ἐρωῇ,
ὣς ἀπὸ θώρηκος Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο
πολλὸν ἀποπλαγχθεὶς ἑκὰς ἔπτατο πικρὸς ὀϊστός.
sentences.l:
And as when from a broad winnowing-shovel over a great threshing-floor
leap dark-skinned beans or chickpeas
under the clear-sounding breath and the winnower’s swing,
so from the breastplate of Menelaus the glorious
far driven off, away flew the bitter arrow.
sentences.i: As when, from a broad winnowing-shovel, dark-skinned beans or chickpeas leap over a great threshing-floor under the clear-sounding breath of the wind and the winnower’s swing, so from the breastplate of glorious Menelaus the bitter arrow was driven far off and flew away.
sentences.n: A simile for the arrow bouncing off the breastplate: the beans and chickpeas that jump off a shovel when grain is winnowed. πτύον is the broad winnowing-shovel with which grain is tossed up so that the wind carries off the chaff; the shovel’s -φιν is an old ending (ἀπὸ πτυόφιν ‘from the shovel’). ἀλωή is the threshing-floor, as at 5.499. θρῴσκωσιν is the subjunctive of θρῴσκω ‘leap’ in a ‘when’-clause; κύαμοι ‘beans’, ἐρέβινθοι ‘chickpeas’, μελανόχροες ‘dark-skinned’. πνοιῇ … λιγυρῇ is the ‘clear-sounding breath’, which the Greek leaves as breath and which can only be the wind; λικμητῆρος is ‘of the winnower’ (from λικμάω ‘winnow’), and ἐρωή is a rush or sweep, here the swing of his throw; ὕπο ‘under’ follows its nouns. ὣς begins the other half: ἀποπλαγχθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀποπλάζω ‘drive off’, πολλόν ‘far’, ἑκάς ‘away’. κυδαλίμοιο ‘glorious’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἄρα χεῖρα βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
τὴν βάλεν ᾗ ῥ’ ἔχε τόξον ἐΰξοον·
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son then the hand, Menelaus good at the war-cry,
that he hit, with which he held the well-polished bow;
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus, Menelaus, good at the war-cry, struck the hand with which Helenus held his well-polished bow;
sentences.n: Menelaus’ cast now hits home: he hits Helenus’ bow-hand, which the Greek picks up with τήν (‘that one’) and the relative ᾗ (‘with which’). χεῖρα is the object, put first; ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle. ἔχε is ἔχε(ν), the imperfect, ‘held’; the subject is Helenus, who is not named. ἐΰξοον ‘well-polished’ is the epithet of a bow. Ἀτρεΐδης … Μενέλαος and βοὴν ἀγαθός are as at 581. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα τόξῳ
ἀντικρὺ διὰ χειρὸς ἐλήλατο χάλκεον ἔγχος.
sentences.l:
and in the bow
straight through the hand had been driven the bronze spear.
sentences.i: and the bronze spear was driven straight through the hand and fixed in the bow.
sentences.n: The spear goes through the hand and into the bow the hand holds, pinning one to the other. ἐν τόξῳ ‘in the bow’ is where the spear is fixed, ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’ and διὰ χειρός ‘through the hand’. ἐλήλατο is the pluperfect passive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, ‘had been driven’, so the sentence says how things stood after the blow. χάλκεον ἔγχος is ‘the bronze spear’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων
χεῖρα παρακρεμάσας·
sentences.l:
and back to the company of his companions he drew away, death-fate avoiding,
his hand having let hang beside him;
sentences.i: and he drew back into the company of his companions, shunning death, with his hand hanging at his side;
sentences.n: Helenus retreats in the same words as Adamas at 566 and Harpalion at 648, the formula translated alike each time. παρακρεμάσας is the aorist participle of παρακρεμάννυμι ‘let hang beside’; the hand hangs because the spear is through it. χεῖρα is its object. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: τὸ δ’ ἐφέλκετο μείλινον ἔγχος.
sentences.l: and that was dragging along, the ashen spear.
sentences.i: and the ashen spear trailed along behind him.
sentences.n: τό ‘that’ points to the spear, which μείλινον ἔγχος ‘the ashen spear’ then names. μείλινον ‘ashen’ means made of ash-wood. ἐφέλκετο is the imperfect middle of ἐφέλκω ‘drag after’, ‘was trailing’; the spear is still through his hand and drags behind him as he goes. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸ μὲν ἐκ χειρὸς ἔρυσεν μεγάθυμος Ἀγήνωρ,
αὐτὴν δὲ ξυνέδησεν ἐϋστρεφεῖ οἰὸς ἀώτῳ
σφενδόνῃ, ἣν ἄρα οἱ θεράπων ἔχε ποιμένι λαῶν.
sentences.l:
And that from the hand drew out great-hearted Agenor,
and the hand itself bound together with well-twisted sheep’s wool,
a sling, which an attendant held for the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: Great-hearted Agenor drew the spear out of the hand and bound the hand with a sling of well-twisted sheep’s wool, which an attendant was carrying for the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: Agenor, a Trojan, helps the wounded Helenus: τὸ μέν ‘that’ is the spear, and αὐτήν ‘the hand itself’ (feminine, agreeing with χεῖρα). ἔρυσεν is the aorist of ἐρύω ‘draw’; ξυνέδησεν ‘bound together’ (ξυν- is the old spelling of συν-). ἀώτῳ is the dative of ἄωτος, a rare word for a tuft or fleece of wool, here the wool the sling is made of; οἰός is the genitive of ὄϊς ‘sheep’. ἐϋστρεφεῖ ‘well-twisted’ (ἐϋ- + στρέφω); σφενδόνῃ ‘sling’ is a second dative, naming what the wool was twisted into. ἔχε is the imperfect, ‘was holding’; θεράπων ‘attendant’. ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Helenus.

sentences.t:
Πείσανδρος δ’ ἰθὺς Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο
ἤϊε·
sentences.l:
And Peisander straight at Menelaus the glorious
went;
sentences.i: And Peisander went straight at glorious Menelaus;
sentences.n: A new fight begins: Peisander, a Trojan, goes against Menelaus; the poem says nothing about him beyond what follows. ἰθύς ‘straight’ takes the genitive Μενελάου: ‘straight at Menelaus’. ἤϊε is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ (3rd singular). κυδαλίμοιο ‘glorious’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄγε μοῖρα κακὴ θανάτοιο τέλος δὲ
σοὶ Μενέλαε δαμῆναι ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι.
sentences.l:
and him led an evil fate of death, and the end,
to be subdued by you, Menelaus, in fearsome fighting.
sentences.i: an evil fate of death led him on, and his end was to be overcome by you, Menelaus, in fearsome fighting.
sentences.n: The poet tells the reader that Peisander is doomed, and turns to speak to Menelaus (σοί, Μενέλαε). μοῖρα κακὴ θανάτοιο is ‘an evil fate of death’, ἄγε the imperfect of ἄγω ‘lead’. The edition prints no stop before τέλος δὲ: as printed, τέλος δέ is ‘and the end’, with δαμῆναι ‘to be subdued’ (aorist passive infinitive of δαμάζω) in apposition and σοί ‘by you’ naming the agent; the same letters can also be read as the single word τέλοσδε, ‘to the end’ (τέλος + the suffix -δε of direction), ‘led him to the end of death’, which comes to the same thing. ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι ‘in fearsome fighting’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες
Ἀτρεΐδης μὲν ἅμαρτε, παραὶ δέ οἱ ἐτράπετ’ ἔγχος,
Πείσανδρος δὲ σάκος Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο
οὔτασεν, οὐδὲ διὰ πρὸ δυνήσατο χαλκὸν ἐλάσσαι·
sentences.l:
And when they were near, going against one another,
Atreus’-son missed, and aside for him turned the spear,
and Peisander the shield of Menelaus the glorious
stabbed, nor was he able to drive the bronze right through;
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, the son of Atreus missed, and the spear turned aside from him, and Peisander stabbed the shield of glorious Menelaus, but could not drive the bronze right through;
sentences.n: Menelaus casts first and misses; Peisander’s spear hits the shield but does not go through. The first line is also 3.15 and the second also 11.232, where Agamemnon is the son of Atreus who misses; here Ἀτρεΐδης is Menelaus, named in the next line but one. The archived text has no stop after ἰόντες. ἅμαρτε is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’; παραί is παρά as an adverb, ‘aside’; ἐτράπετ’ is ἐτράπετο, ‘turned’; οἱ ‘from him’ (Peisander). οὔτασεν is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘stab’. διὰ πρό ‘right through’; δυνήσατο ‘was able’; ἐλάσσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’ with the double σ.

sentences.t:
ἔσχεθε γὰρ σάκος εὐρύ, κατεκλάσθη δ’ ἐνὶ καυλῷ
ἔγχος· ὃ δὲ φρεσὶν ᾗσι χάρη καὶ ἐέλπετο νίκην.
sentences.l:
for the broad shield held, and was broken in the socket
the spear; and he in his own wits rejoiced and hoped for victory.
sentences.i: for the broad shield held, and the spear snapped in the socket; but he rejoiced in his own mind and hoped for victory.
sentences.n: Peisander’s spear breaks against the shield, and he is pleased all the same, wrongly, as the next unit shows. ἔσχεθε is the aorist of ἔχω with an added -θ-, here without an object, ‘held, held firm’; σάκος εὐρύ ‘the broad shield’ is its subject (the nominative and accusative of σάκος are alike, and I take it as the subject). κατεκλάσθη is the aorist passive of κατακλάω ‘break off’. καυλός is ‘stem’; of a spear it is usually taken as the socket where the head sits on the shaft, but the word itself says only ‘stem’. ὃ δέ ‘but he’ is Peisander. φρεσὶν ᾗσι ‘in his own wits’ (ᾗσι is the possessive ‘own’), χάρη ‘rejoiced’ (the aorist passive of χαίρω without augment), ἐέλπετο ‘was hoping’, the imperfect of ἔλπομαι.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ ἐρυσσάμενος ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον
ἆλτ’ ἐπὶ Πεισάνδρῳ·
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son, drawing his silver-studded sword,
leapt upon Peisander;
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus drew his silver-studded sword and leapt on Peisander;
sentences.n: Menelaus, his cast gone, draws his sword; the first line recurs at 3.361, where it is also Menelaus. ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’; ἀργυρόηλον is ‘silver-studded’ (the sword with silver nails or studs). ἆλτ’ is ἆλτο, the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and ἐπὶ Πεισάνδρῳ is ‘at Peisander’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος εἵλετο καλὴν
ἀξίνην εὔχαλκον ἐλαΐνῳ ἀμφὶ πελέκκῳ
μακρῷ ἐϋξέστῳ·
sentences.i: and he took from under his shield a fine axe of good bronze, set on a long, well-polished handle of olive wood;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Peisander, who has kept an axe under his shield for the close fight. ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος ‘from under the shield’, εἵλετο ‘took’. ἀξίνη is an axe, εὔχαλκος ‘of good bronze’ describes its head. πέλεκκον is the problem: the usual word for an axe is πέλεκυς, and ἀξίνη already means ‘axe’, so here it can only be the thing the head is set on, the handle, with ἀμφί ‘about’ giving the setting; that sense is taken from the context and is not certain. ἐλαΐνῳ ‘of olive wood’, μακρῷ ‘long’, ἐϋξέστῳ ‘well-polished’ agree with it. The unit begins and ends in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἅμα δ’ ἀλλήλων ἐφίκοντο.
sentences.l: and together of one another they got hold.
sentences.i: and they reached each other at the same moment.
sentences.n: ἅμα ‘at the same time’; ἐφίκοντο is the imperfect of ἐφικνέομαι ‘reach, get at’, which takes the genitive ἀλλήλων. Both blows land at once, and the next unit gives them. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν κόρυθος φάλον ἤλασεν ἱπποδασείης
ἄκρον ὑπὸ λόφον αὐτόν, ὃ δὲ προσιόντα μέτωπον
ῥινὸς ὕπερ πυμάτης·
sentences.i: The one struck the ridge of the helmet, thick with horsehair, at the top, just under the crest itself, and the other struck him as he came on, on the forehead, just above the bridge of the nose;
sentences.n: Both strikes at once: Peisander’s axe lands on Menelaus’ helmet and Menelaus’ sword on Peisander’s forehead. The Greek says only ὃ μέν … ὃ δέ ‘the one … the other’; the sequel shows who is who, since it is Peisander whose eyes fall out (616–617) and Menelaus who speaks over him (619–620). ἤτοι ‘truly’; κόρυθος φάλον ἱπποδασείης is ‘the ridge of the helmet, thick with horsehair’ (φάλος, sense not certain, taken as the ridge), and ἄκρον ὑπὸ λόφον αὐτόν is ‘at the top, under the crest itself’. In the second half ἤλασεν is understood from the first. προσιόντα ‘as he came on’ is an accusative masculine participle, ‘him coming on’, and μέτωπον ‘the forehead’ is the part struck. ῥινὸς ὕπερ πυμάτης is ‘above the last (part) of the nose’: πύματος means ‘last’, and the part of the nose that stands under the forehead is meant. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
λάκε δ’ ὀστέα, τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε
πὰρ ποσὶν αἱματόεντα χαμαὶ πέσον ἐν κονίῃσιν,
ἰδνώθη δὲ πεσών·
sentences.i: and the bones cracked, and both his eyes, bloody, fell to the ground in the dust beside his feet; and he doubled up as he fell;
sentences.n: Menelaus’ sword has broken through Peisander’s forehead. λάκε is the aorist of λάσκω ‘crack, crash’, without augment; ὀστέα ‘bones’. τώ … ὄσσε is the dual ‘his two eyes’ (the pair); οἱ ‘his’; αἱματόεντα ‘bloody’; πὰρ ποσίν ‘beside his feet’ (πάρ is παρά) and ἐν κονίῃσιν ‘in the dust’ (the plural dative of κονίη). ἰδνώθη is the aorist passive of ἰδνόομαι ‘double up, bend over’; πεσών ‘having fallen’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ λὰξ ἐν στήθεσι βαίνων
τεύχεά τ’ ἐξενάριξε καὶ εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.l:
and he, with his heel on his chest, stepping,
despoiled the armour, and, declaring, spoke a word:
sentences.i: and he, setting his heel on his chest, stripped off his armour and said, declaring aloud:
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Menelaus, who now speaks. λάξ ‘with the heel’, ἐν στήθεσι ‘on the chest’ (a plural for one chest) and βαίνων ‘stepping’ give the stance of a victor over a corpse. τεύχεα ‘armour’ is the object of ἐξενάριξε, the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip’; the killing has been told, so only the stripping is rendered. εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα ‘declaring, spoke a word’: εὔχομαι is here ‘declare, vaunt’, not ‘pray’, and ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’. The speech follows, with no marks in the Greek. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
λείψετέ θην οὕτω γε νέας Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων
Τρῶες ὑπερφίαλοι δεινῆς ἀκόρητοι ἀϋτῆς,
ἄλλης μὲν λώβης τε καὶ αἴσχεος οὐκ ἐπιδευεῖς
ἣν ἐμὲ λωβήσασθε κακαὶ κύνες, οὐδέ τι θυμῷ
Ζηνὸς ἐριβρεμέτεω χαλεπὴν ἐδείσατε μῆνιν
ξεινίου, ὅς τέ ποτ’ ὔμμι διαφθέρσει πόλιν αἰπήν·
sentences.l:
“You will leave, I think, in this way at least, the ships of the swift-colted Danaans,
Trojans overweening, insatiate of dread battle-cry,
not lacking in other outrage and shame,
which you did to me, evil dogs, and not at all in your spirit
of Zeus loud-rumbling did you fear the harsh wrath,
the god of guests, who some day will destroy for you your steep city;
sentences.i: “This is how you will leave the ships of the Danaans with their swift colts, I think, you overweening Trojans who cannot have enough of the dread battle-cry, who are not short of other outrage and shame, the outrage you did me, evil dogs, and did not fear in your heart the harsh wrath of loud-rumbling Zeus, the god of guests, who will one day destroy your steep city;
sentences.n: Menelaus speaks over Peisander, to the Trojans. λείψετε is the future of λείπω ‘leave’, here ‘abandon’; θην ‘I think, surely’; οὕτω γε ‘in this way at least’ points to the dead man at his feet, and the Greek does not say more about how the Trojans will leave the ships. Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων ‘of the Danaans with swift colts’, νέας the accusative plural of ναῦς ‘ships’, Τρῶες the Trojans addressed (nominative for the vocative). ὑπερφίαλοι ‘overweening’, ἀκόρητοι ‘insatiate’ with the genitive δεινῆς ἀϋτῆς ‘dread battle-cry’. ἄλλης … λώβης τε καὶ αἴσχεος οὐκ ἐπιδευεῖς ‘not lacking in other outrage and shame’ (ἐπιδευής takes the genitive), and ἣν … λωβήσασθε ‘which you outraged me with’ (λωβάομαι ‘do outrage to’, with the outrage itself as cognate object). κακαὶ κύνες ‘evil dogs’ is an insult, with the adjective feminine. οὐδέ τι θυμῷ ‘nor at all in your spirit’; ἐδείσατε is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’. Ζηνός is the epic genitive of Ζεύς; ἐριβρεμέτης ‘loud-rumbling’ is a rare epithet of Zeus (ἐρι- ‘loud’ + βρέμω ‘roar’); χαλεπήν ‘harsh’; ξεινίου ‘of the god of guests’ agrees with Ζηνός. ὅς τε ‘who’, ὔμμι ‘for you’ (ὑμῖν), διαφθέρσει ‘will destroy’ (future of διαφθείρω), πόλιν αἰπήν ‘steep city’. ξεινίου fits the charge that comes next, that the Trojans abused the welcome they had received. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οἵ μευ κουριδίην ἄλοχον καὶ κτήματα πολλὰ
μὰψ οἴχεσθ’ ἀνάγοντες, ἐπεὶ φιλέεσθε παρ’ αὐτῇ·
sentences.l:
who my wedded wife and many possessions
recklessly have gone off carrying away, when you were being befriended beside her;
sentences.i: you who went off recklessly, carrying away my wedded wife and many possessions, when you were being treated as friends beside her;
sentences.n: The charge is the theft of Helen. μευ is μου ‘my’ (epic); κουριδίην ἄλοχον ‘the wedded wife’ is Helen, and κτήματα ‘possessions’. οἴχεσθε is the present of οἴχομαι ‘be gone, have gone off’, and with ἀνάγοντες ‘carrying away’ (ἀνάγω ‘lead up, take up to the ships’) it says ‘you have gone off carrying’; μάψ ‘recklessly’. ἐπεὶ φιλέεσθε παρ’ αὐτῇ: φιλέεσθε is φιλεῖσθε, the present passive of φιλέω ‘treat as a friend’, and παρ’ αὐτῇ ‘beside her’, in her company; ἐπεί may mean ‘since’ or ‘when’, and the English takes ‘when’. The Greek does not say whose house it was.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτ’ ἐν νηυσὶν μενεαίνετε ποντοπόροισι
πῦρ ὀλοὸν βαλέειν, κτεῖναι δ’ ἥρωας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
Now again on the sea-crossing ships you are eager
deadly fire to throw, and to kill the hero Achaeans.
sentences.i: Now, again, you are eager to hurl deadly fire on the sea-crossing ships and to kill the Achaean heroes.
sentences.n: From the old wrong to the present attack. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again’, and μενεαίνετε ‘you are eager, you are bent on’ takes two infinitives: βαλέειν (epic for βαλεῖν) ‘to throw, hurl’ and κτεῖναι ‘to kill’. ἐν νηυσίν ‘on the ships’ (νηυσί is the epic dative plural of ναῦς), ποντοπόροισι ‘sea-crossing’, πῦρ ὀλοόν ‘deadly fire’. ἥρωας Ἀχαιούς ‘the hero Achaeans’ calls the army heroes.

sentences.t: ἀλλά ποθι σχήσεσθε καὶ ἐσσύμενοί περ Ἄρηος.
sentences.l: But somewhere you will hold back, even though hurrying for Ares.
sentences.i: But hold back you will, somewhere, eager as you are for war.
sentences.n: A prediction: the Trojans will be stopped. ποθι is που ‘somewhere’, here ‘at some point, sooner or later’. σχήσεσθε is the future middle of ἔχω, ‘you will hold yourselves back’. ἐσσύμενοι is the participle of σεύομαι, ‘hurrying, eager’, with περ ‘although’ and the genitive Ἄρηος: Ἄρης (the god) stands for war, and the English says ‘war’.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ἦ τέ σέ φασι περὶ φρένας ἔμμεναι ἄλλων
ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ θεῶν·
sentences.l:
Father Zeus, truly they say that you in wits surpass others,
men and gods;
sentences.i: Father Zeus, they do say that you surpass all other men and gods in mind;
sentences.n: Menelaus turns from the Trojans to Zeus. Ζεῦ πάτερ ‘Father Zeus’; ἦ τέ ‘truly, indeed’; φασί ‘they say’. περὶ … ἔμμεναι ἄλλων is ‘to be above the others’, ‘to surpass them’: ἔμμεναι is εἶναι, περί governs the genitive ἄλλων ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ θεῶν ‘other men and gods’, and φρένας is an accusative of respect, ‘in wits’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: σέο δ’ ἐκ τάδε πάντα πέλονται·
sentences.l: and from you all these things come about;
sentences.i: and all this comes from you;
sentences.n: Everything that happens has Zeus behind it, which is what Menelaus is about to complain of. σέο is the epic genitive of σύ ‘you’, and ἐκ follows it (‘from you’). πάντα ‘all’ and πέλονται ‘come about, come to be’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οἷον δὴ ἄνδρεσσι χαρίζεαι ὑβριστῇσι
Τρωσίν, τῶν μένος αἰὲν ἀτάσθαλον, οὐδὲ δύνανται
φυλόπιδος κορέσασθαι ὁμοιΐου πτολέμοιο.
sentences.l:
How indeed you show favour to violent men,
the Trojans, whose might is ever wanton, and they cannot
have their fill of the battle-din of war common to all.
sentences.i: How you favour violent men, the Trojans, whose might is ever wanton, and who cannot have their fill of the battle-din of the war that is common to all.
sentences.n: The complaint to Zeus: he favours men who do not deserve it. οἷον δή is exclamatory, ‘how!’, and χαρίζεαι is χαρίζῃ, second person of χαρίζομαι ‘show favour to’, with the dative ἄνδρεσσι (epic) ὑβριστῇσι ‘violent’. τῶν is the relative ‘whose’; μένος ‘might’; ἀτάσθαλον ‘wanton’. κορέσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of κορέννυμι ‘satisfy’, ‘to have one’s fill’, and takes the genitive φυλόπιδος ‘battle-din’. ὁμοίϊος πόλεμος ‘war common to all’: the sense of ὁμοίϊος is not certain (‘even-handed’ is the other guess), and the English keeps to ‘common to all’ as at 9.440.

sentences.t:
πάντων μὲν κόρος ἐστὶ καὶ ὕπνου καὶ φιλότητος
μολπῆς τε γλυκερῆς καὶ ἀμύμονος ὀρχηθμοῖο,
τῶν πέρ τις καὶ μᾶλλον ἐέλδεται ἐξ ἔρον εἷναι
ἢ πολέμου·
sentences.l:
Of all things there is satiety, and of sleep and of love,
and of sweet song-and-dance and of blameless dancing,
of which anyone even more wishes to put away desire
than of war;
sentences.i: Of everything there comes a fullness, of sleep and love and sweet song and dance and blameless dancing; anyone longs to have his fill even more of these than of war;
sentences.n: The argument is that men tire of the pleasures of life, but the Trojans cannot tire of fighting (the next unit). κόρος is ‘satiety, having had enough’; μολπῆς … γλυκερῆς καὶ ἀμύμονος ὀρχηθμοῖο ‘sweet song-and-dance and blameless dancing’ is also a line of the Odyssey (23.145), and ἀμύμων is ‘blameless’. τῶν πέρ τις καὶ μᾶλλον ἐέλδεται: ‘of which anyone even more longs’, with ἐέλδεται ‘longs, wishes’. ἐξ ἔρον εἷναι is a set phrase in which εἷναι is the aorist infinitive of ἵημι (as in ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο ‘they had put away desire’, the Odyssey’s meal formula), so ‘to put away desire’, ‘to have had one’s fill’. ἢ πολέμου ‘than of war’ ends the unit at the ano teleia in mid-line. The sentence is hard to put into English; the sense given is the one the Greek supports.

sentences.t: Τρῶες δὲ μάχης ἀκόρητοι ἔασιν.
sentences.l: but the Trojans are insatiate of battle.”
sentences.i: but the Trojans cannot have enough of battle.”
sentences.n: The contrast that closes the speech. Τρῶες … ἀκόρητοι ‘the Trojans … insatiate’, with the genitive μάχης ‘of battle’, as the same adjective stood at 621 with ἀϋτῆς; ἔασιν is εἰσίν. The speech ends here. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν τὰ μὲν ἔντε’ ἀπὸ χροὸς αἱματόεντα
συλήσας ἑτάροισι δίδου Μενέλαος ἀμύμων,
αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ ἐξ αὖτις ἰὼν προμάχοισιν ἐμίχθη.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, the gear, bloody, from the body
having stripped, to his companions he gave it, Menelaus blameless,
and himself again, back again going, among the front-fighters mingled.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and stripped the bloody gear from the body and gave it to his companions, blameless Menelaus; and he himself went back again to mingle with the foremost fighters.
sentences.n: Menelaus has finished speaking. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’. τὰ … ἔντε’ is τὰ ἔντεα, ‘the gear’, the armour and arms taken from the dead man, αἱματόεντα ‘bloody’, ἀπὸ χροός ‘from the body’ (χρώς ‘flesh, skin’). συλήσας is the aorist participle of συλάω ‘strip’, and δίδου the imperfect of δίδωμι ‘give’. ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet. αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ ἐξ αὖτις ἰών ‘and himself again, going back again’, with προμάχοισιν ἐμίχθη ‘mingled with the front-fighters’, as at 5.134.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά οἱ υἱὸς ἐπᾶλτο Πυλαιμένεος βασιλῆος
Ἁρπαλίων, ὅ ῥα πατρὶ φίλῳ ἕπετο πτολεμίξων
ἐς τροίην, οὐδ’ αὖτις ἀφίκετο πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.i: Then the son of King Pylaemenes leapt upon him, Harpalion, who had followed his dear father to Troy to fight, and he did not come back to his fatherland;
sentences.n: A new fighter: Harpalion, son of King Pylaemenes, the leader of the Paphlagonians at 2.851. οἱ ‘upon him’ is Menelaus. ἐπᾶλτο is the aorist of ἐφάλλομαι ‘leap upon’. ὅ ῥα is ‘who’ with a particle; ἕπετο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’; πτολεμίξων is the future participle of πτολεμίζω ‘fight’, giving the purpose (‘to fight’). ἐς τροίην is printed with a small τ in the pinned text and is read as ‘to Troy’. οὐδ’ αὖτις ἀφίκετο πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘nor did he come again to his fatherland’ tells the reader he will die here. βασιλῆος is the epic genitive of βασιλεύς ‘king’.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥα τότ’ Ἀτρεΐδαο μέσον σάκος οὔτασε δουρὶ
ἐγγύθεν, οὐδὲ διὰ πρὸ δυνήσατο χαλκὸν ἐλάσσαι
ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων
πάντοσε παπταίνων μή τις χρόα χαλκῷ ἐπαύρῃ.
sentences.l:
who then the middle of Atreus’-son’s shield stabbed with his spear
from close by, nor was he able to drive the bronze right through;
and back to the company of his companions he drew away, death-fate avoiding,
glancing everywhere, lest someone touch his skin with bronze.
sentences.i: He stabbed the middle of the shield of the son of Atreus with his spear from close by, but could not drive the bronze right through; and he drew back into the company of his companions, shunning death, glancing about on every side lest anyone touch his skin with bronze.
sentences.n: Harpalion does what Adamas and Helenus did: a thrust, a failure, a retreat. ὅς ῥα τότ’ ‘who then’ continues the account of Harpalion. Ἀτρεΐδαο is the epic genitive of Ἀτρεΐδης, Menelaus; μέσον σάκος ‘the middle of the shield’, as at 561. 647 is as 607 and 648 is the formula of 566 and 596. The archived text has no stop after ἐλάσσαι or after ἀλεείνων, so the unit runs on to 649. πάντοσε παπταίνων ‘glancing about on every side’ (παπταίνω ‘glance about’); μή τις … ἐπαύρῃ ‘lest anyone touch’ is a fear clause with the aorist subjunctive of ἐπαυρίσκω ‘touch’; χρόα is the accusative of χρώς.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δ’ ἀπιόντος ἵει χαλκήρε’ ὀϊστόν,
καί ῥ’ ἔβαλε γλουτὸν κάτα δεξιόν·
sentences.l:
And Meriones, at him going away, let fly a bronze-fitted arrow,
and hit him on the right buttock;
sentences.i: And Meriones let fly a bronze-fitted arrow at him as he went away, and hit him in the right buttock;
sentences.n: Meriones, who killed Adamas at 567, now shoots Harpalion as he retreats. ἀπιόντος ‘him going away’ is a genitive participle, after ἵει, the imperfect of ἵημι ‘let fly’. χαλκήρε’ is χαλκήρεα, ‘bronze-fitted’, elided; ὀϊστός ‘arrow’. καί ῥ’ is καὶ ἄρα; ἔβαλε ‘hit’; γλουτόν ‘buttock’, κάτα is κατά placed after its noun. δεξιόν ‘right’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὀϊστὸς
ἀντικρὺ κατὰ κύστιν ὑπ’ ὀστέον ἐξεπέρησεν.
sentences.l:
but the arrow
straight through the bladder, below the bone, passed right out.
sentences.i: and the arrow went straight through the bladder, under the bone, and out the other side.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but, and’ continues from the hit. ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’; κατὰ κύστιν ὑπ’ ὀστέον ‘through the bladder, below the bone’ is also said at 5.67; the Greek says only ‘the bone’. ἐξεπέρησεν is the aorist of ἐκπεράω ‘pass right through and out’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἑζόμενος δὲ κατ’ αὖθι φίλων ἐν χερσὶν ἑταίρων
θυμὸν ἀποπνείων, ὥς τε σκώληξ ἐπὶ γαίῃ
κεῖτο ταθείς·
sentences.i: Sitting down there, in the hands of his dear companions, breathing out his life, he lay stretched on the earth like a worm;
sentences.n: Harpalion’s death. ἑζόμενος ‘sitting down’ (the aorist of ἕζομαι) shows him sinking down among his companions’ hands before he lies stretched out; κατ’ αὖθι is ‘on the very spot’. θυμὸν ἀποπνείων ‘breathing out his life’: θυμός here is the life that leaves a man. ὥς τε σκώληξ ‘like a worm’; the Greek says only ‘worm’. κεῖτο ταθείς ‘lay stretched out’ (ταθείς is the aorist passive participle of τείνω ‘stretch’). The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ αἷμα μέλαν ῥέε, δεῦε δὲ γαῖαν.
sentences.l: and out the black blood flowed, and wet the earth.
sentences.i: and black blood flowed out and soaked the earth.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ῥέε is split in two (a tmesis): ‘flowed out’, from ῥέω. δεῦε is the imperfect of δεύω ‘wet, drench’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν Παφλαγόνες μεγαλήτορες ἀμφεπένοντο,
ἐς δίφρον δ’ ἀνέσαντες ἄγον προτὶ Ἴλιον ἱρὴν
ἀχνύμενοι·
sentences.i: The great-spirited Paphlagonians busied themselves about him, and, lifting him into a chariot, took him to sacred Ilium, grieving;
sentences.n: τόν is Harpalion; the Paphlagonians are his father’s people (2.851). ἀμφεπένοντο is an imperfect of ἀμφιπένομαι ‘busy oneself about’ (the middle of ἀμφιέπω). ἀνέσαντες is an aorist participle whose dictionary form I cannot confirm; from ἀν- ‘up’ and the context it means ‘having put up’, here into the chariot (ἐς δίφρον). ἄγον ‘led, took’; προτὶ Ἴλιον ἱρήν ‘to sacred Ilium’. μεγαλήτορες ‘great-spirited’ and ἀχνύμενοι ‘grieving’ are the participle and epithet as in the table. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δέ σφι πατὴρ κίε δάκρυα λείβων,
ποινὴ δ’ οὔ τις παιδὸς ἐγίγνετο τεθνηῶτος.
sentences.l:
and among them went his father, pouring out tears,
but no requital for the child was coming about, now dead.
sentences.i: and with them went his father, pouring out his tears; but no requital was coming for his dead son.
sentences.n: The part ends on the father’s grief. μετά … σφι is ‘with them’, κίε the imperfect of κίω ‘go’, and δάκρυα λείβων ‘pouring out tears’. ποινή is ‘requital’, what is paid or exacted for a death; the line says that none came about for the dead boy (παιδὸς τεθνηῶτος, ‘the dead child’, where τεθνηῶτος is the epic perfect participle of θνήσκω), and does not say how it might have come. ἐγίγνετο is the imperfect of γίγνομαι ‘come about, be forthcoming’.
